column4: The section says the womb is where Allah forms a child as He wills; this ayah says Mary guarded her chastity and Allah made her and her son a sign, placing divine care in a specific mother-and-child story.
The section follows a child from the womb through formation; this ayah recalls the human beginning as a drop of emitted fluid.
The section describes growth state by state; this ayah names the next stage, the drop becoming a clinging form.
The section's image makes divine formation in the womb perceptible; this ayah says Allah formed and proportioned the human and made from him male and female.
The section takes the child from an enclosed beginning toward completion; this ayah asks what the human was created from, opening a passage about formation.
The section makes the womb the first home of a growing child; this ayah says the human was created from a drop and then measured.
The section describes care as carrying a child from one state to another; this ayah says Allah made the human's path easy after creation.
The section defines upbringing as bringing something through states toward completion; this ayah traces human life from weakness to strength and then weakness and old age.
The section extends upbringing into learning; this ayah tells Yahya to take the Scripture firmly while still a child.
The section defines raḥmah as tenderness leading to good; this ayah describes Yahya as receiving tenderness (حَنَانًا) and purity from Allah.
The section joins the child's upbringing to later care for parents; this ayah says Yahya was dutiful to his parents and not arrogant or rebellious.
The section's Moses image shows a child protected and raised; this ayah supplies the danger around his infancy, as Pharaoh oppressed the people and slaughtered their sons.
The section says mercy attends a vulnerable child; this ayah says Allah intended to favor those oppressed in the land and make them leaders and inheritors.

After 28:5 states favor for the oppressed, this ayah says Allah would establish them in the land and show Pharaoh and his people what they feared, completing the reversal of Pharaoh's power over Moses' family.
The section links a household with children and its material sustenance; this ayah says Allah made spouses, sons, and grandchildren for people and provided good things.
The section's image makes adults responsible for the vulnerable child; this ayah warns people to fear leaving behind weak offspring and to speak rightly about them.
The section says mercy becomes good treatment, especially for the weak and kin; this ayah joins goodness to parents and relatives with care for orphans and the needy.
The section connects kinship to practical care; this ayah includes spending on relatives, orphans, the needy, and the traveler among acts of righteousness.
The section describes mercy as tenderness toward the weak; this ayah rebukes the opposite conduct, failing to honor an orphan.
The section says care should become concrete help for the vulnerable; this ayah rebukes failing to urge the feeding of the needy.
The section explains kinship through people emerging from one womb; this ayah says blood relatives are closer to one another in Allah's decree.
The section links a mother's bodily labor with a child's upbringing and care; this ayah commands goodness to parents and recalls the mother's hardship in carrying and weaning.
The section includes a child raised by someone other than a birth parent; this ayah says improving orphans' affairs is best and describes them as brothers when their lives are joined.

The section's household image centers on sustaining a vulnerable child; this ayah forbids guardians from consuming or exchanging orphans' property, marking a boundary against exploiting those in their care.

The section presents a child's home as a place of nurture; this ayah gives a difficult boundary in the Moses-and-Khidr account, where the boy's future conduct is feared to burden his believing parents.

After 18:80 explains the feared harm to the parents, this ayah states the hope that their Lord replace the boy with one better in purity and nearer to affection, framing a severe act as protection for the family.
The section extends rabb's upbringing sense to teaching; this ayah shows Moses asking Khidr to teach him from the knowledge Allah had given Khidr.
The section describes teaching as a form of nurture; this ayah says the Messenger recites, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom to the community.
The section's dictionary sense of rabb as a teacher who nourishes people with knowledge has an ethical boundary here: rabbāniyyūn and scholars are rebuked for not forbidding wrongdoing.
The section says a teacher feeds people small units of knowledge; this ayah describes some believers studying religion so they can warn and teach their people when they return.
The section connects child-rearing with instruction; Luqman begins addressing his son with foundational guidance against associating partners with Allah.
The section places upbringing within a family relation; this ayah tells a child to remain companionably kind to parents even when refusing their demand to associate partners with Allah.
The section's teacher develops a child's understanding; Luqman teaches his son that even a tiny deed hidden in a rock or the heavens or earth is known to Allah.
The section extends rabb's care into teaching; Luqman instructs his son in prayer, good conduct, and patience.
The section depicts upbringing as preparing a child for life among others; Luqman teaches his son not to turn away from people or walk arrogantly.
The section describes education as developing capacities over time; Luqman gives his son practical counsel on his pace and voice.

The section pictures the household as a place of care and protection; this ayah marks a boundary by warning that some spouses and children may oppose a believer, while commanding pardon and forbearance.
The section notes children raised in comfort; this ayah warns that wealth and children are a trial, limiting any assumption that household provision itself proves spiritual good.
The section defines tarbiya as moving something state by state; this ayah says people will pass from one state to another, extending that staged-life image beyond childhood.

The section describes a household's care and provision for relatives and vulnerable people; this ayah instructs that relatives, orphans, and the needy present at an inheritance division receive something from it.
